McMinnville Airport ASOS recorded a peak wind gust of 48 mph. Public reported multiple trees down south of Dayton, and a tree down west of Carlton.

A weather station at Cape Disappointment recorded a max sustained wind of 56 mph with a peak gust of 72 mph. Other stations along the South Washington Coast recorded wind gusts peaking around 55 to 70 mph.
Strong thunderstorm produced a gust to 59 mph at a weather station located in Cannon Beach.
Strong thunderstorm produced winds gusting up to 59 mph, recorded at a weather station at Gleneden Beach.
Thunderstorms produced strong winds on and off through the morning, with the strongest gust of 63 mph at Cape Disappointment.
Abernathy RAWS weather station recorded wind gusts up to 63 mph.
Weather station at Yachats reported a peak gust of 69 mph. Other stations reported peak gusts of 59 mph to 63 mph.

A weather station at Mt. Hebo recorded a peak gust of 59 mph. Another report in a nearby zone reported wind gusts of 61 mph along Chehalem road. The Oregon Department of Transportation reported downed trees across Highway 18 near Grande Ronde, closing the road at milepost 21.

events.cz_name: CENTRAL COAST RANGE OF W OREGON
events.event_narrative: Rockhouse RAWS weather station reported a peak gust of 60 mph. On top of Mary's Peak, approximately 3,000 feet in the Coast Range, a peak gust of 102 mph was recorded. A trained spotter reported a 5 inch diameter Cherry Tree and an 80 year old apple tree toppled. Many 2 inch branches scattered around the area.  Oregon Department of Transportation reported that Highway 18 was closed at milepost 21 due to downed trees.
Cape Disappointment measured a peak gust of 65 mph, with sustained winds at 53 mph.

events.cz_name: CENTRAL COAST RANGE OF W OREGON
events.event_narrative: A weather station at Mary's Peak, elevation approximately 4000 feet,  measured sustained winds up to 59 mph with gusts peaking at 92 mph.  In an adjacent zone, the broadcast media also reported a trees down along Chehalem Valley road.

Strong winds brought many trees down across the area. Over 20,000 customers were without power. Downed trees blocked roads, fell on houses, and took down power lines. Wind or falling trees also snapped power poles in a few areas. Light rail service was disrupted due to power outages and downed trees.
Strong winds downed many trees that blocked several local roads across the Vancouver Metro area.

Heavy rain resulted in flooding of the Grays River near Rosburg. Grays River reached flood stage at 1021 AM on November 24th, and crested at 13.9 feet at 1215 AM November 25th. The river dropped below flood stage at 850 AM November 25th.

Heavy rain resulted in flooding of the Tualatin River at Dilley. The Tualatin River reached flood stage at 730 AM on November 25th, and crested at 17.7 feet at 1215 PM on November 25th. The river dropped below flood stage at 640 PM on November 25.

Heavy rain resulted in flooding of the Nehalem River near Foss. The Nehalem River reached flood stage at 100 AM on November 25th, and crested at 15.2 feet at 300 AM on November 25th. The river dropped below flood stage at 750 AM on November 25.

Heavy rain resulted in flooding of the South Yamhill River at McMinnville. The South Yamhill River reached flood stage at 1253 AM on November 26th, and crested at 51.8 feet at 700 AM on November 26th. The river dropped below flood stage at 655 PM on November 27.

Heavy rain resulted in flooding of the Marys River near Philomath. The Marys River reached flood stage at 205 AM on November 25th, and crested at 21.2 feet at 1030 AM on November 25th. The river dropped below flood stage at 800 AM on November 26.

Heavy rain resulted in flooding of the Siletz River at Siletz. The Siletz River reached flood stage at 115 AM on November 25th, and crested at 16.5 feet at 345 AM on November 25th. The river dropped below flood stage at 715 AM on November 25.

Heavy rain resulted in flooding of the Luckiamute River near Suver. The Luckiamute River reached flood stage at 1225 PM on November 25th, and crested at 28.8 feet at 830 PM on November 25th. The river dropped below flood stage at 627 PM on November 26.

Heavy rain resulted in flooding of the Wilson River near Tillamook. The Wilson River reached flood stage at 1053 PM on November 24th, and crested at 12.5 feet at 130 AM on November 25th. The river dropped below flood stage at 428 AM on November 25.

Heavy rain resulted in flooding of the Nehalem River near Vernonia. The Nehalem River reached flood stage at 915 PM on November 24th, and crested at 12.5 feet at 1246 AM on November 25th. The river dropped below flood stage at 418 AM on November 25.
A weather station on the Astoria/Megler Bridge recorded sustained winds up to 45 mph.
A weather station on the Astoria/Megler Bridge recorded sustained winds up to 45 mph.
A weather station at Pacific City recorded sustained winds up to 46 mph during the morning of the event. Later in the day, a weather station at Cannon Beach recorded wind gusts up to 65 mph.
Earlier in the event, the Newport AWOS recorded wind gusts up to 59 mph. Later, weather stations at Yachats and Gleneden Beach recorded wind gusts up to 60 mph.
A weather station at Cape Disappointment recorded wind gusts up to 58 mph.
The Abernathy RAWS site recorded wind gusts up to 60 mph.

This fire burned uncontained through all of August into September, and was not expected to be contained until the Fall rains in October.

The fire caused I-84 to close for 19 days from September 4th through September 23rd, and the Historic Columbia River Highway will likely remain closed for months in this area.

The tornado started on Boones Ferry Rd NE, west of the Aurora airport. Greenhouses in the area sustained damage, and the tornado continued to travel east across the airport property. Two planes were flipped at Willamette Aviation Services. The tornado ended near Airport Rd NE.
Heavy rain, with amounts up to 10.7 inches in the Coast Range led to flooding on the Wilson River near Tillamook. The river crested at 17.05 feet, which is 5.05 feet above flood stage.
Heavy rain caused the Clackamas River near Estacada to flood. The river crested at 21.40 feet, which is 1.40 ft above flood stage.
Heavy rain caused the Nehalem River near Foss to flood. The river crested at 15.02 feet, which is 0.02 foot above flood stage.
Heavy rain caused the Siletz River at Siletz to flood. The river crested at 19.07 feet, which is 3.07 feet above flood stage.
Heavy rain caused the Trask River near Tillamook to flood. The river crested at 17.56 feet, which is 1.06 feet above flood stage.

Heavy rain caused the Washougal River at Washougal to flood. The river crested at 14.97 feet, which is 0.97 foot above flood stage.

Weather stations on Yaquina Bridge and in Yachats recorded sustained winds up to 47 to 49 mph.

Several trees and some power lines were blown down.  One tree fell into a house in Corbett, injuring one person.

Strong winds that persisted for several days took a few limbs off trees, took a few shingles off at least one roof, and knocked over a couple fences in the Troutdale area near the Columbia River Gorge.  The Troutdale Airport ASOS recorded wind gusts up to 46 mph on 12/8.

Pepper Creek SNOTEL reported 8 inches of snow from this event.

NWAC snow observation at Timberline Lodge (5880 ft) reported 19 inches. Bear Grass SNOTEL (4720 ft) reported 17 inches, with 15 inches over a 12 hour period. Many other sites reported 10 to 15 inches of snow.
CoCoRaHS Observer near McKenzie Bridge at 1500 feet recorded 8.2 inches of snow from this event.

The NWS Observation recorded 1 inch of snow, which was similar to most locations around north Portland, with some areas farther south only getting around 0.2 inch. Snow turned to freezing rain, with a total of 0.15 inch of ice at the NWS Office.

A mix of spotters and local public reported 1 to 3 inches of snow around the Vancouver area, with highest amounts north around Ridgefield. Clatsop County emergency manager reported severe beach erosion and damage to trails near the Peter Iredale Shipwreck, northward to south Jetty. About 5 to 6 feet of dune entirely eroded and swept out to sea. Tillamook Emergency manager reported Seaside and Cannon Beach had water in streets. Logs and other debris washed up on closed roads. In Neskowin, a hotel prepared ahead of time and had minimal loss from flooding of bottom floor.

A restaurant in Lincoln City struck by large waves tearing out a gas line and knocking out power.  A hotel in Lincoln City damaged on bottom floor from waves crashing into the hotel. Damage to condos in Lincoln City. The Inn at Spanish Head sustained significant damage to building and swimming pool.
Picture on Twitter from Seaside showed 2 inch hail. A trained spotter also reported 1 inch hail 1 mile north of Seaside.
Weather station on Cape Disappointment recorded wind gusts up to 67 mph.

The day after the snow on February 22nd, a woman who was delivering newspapers died after she was pinned underneath her car on a steep icy Astoria street.  Astoria saw around 1 inch of snow from this event.
SNOTEL sites and NWAC stations above 3,000 feet recorded anywhere from 13 to 18 inches of snow from this event, with highest amounts at higher elevations, generally above 5,000 feet.

Pinto Rock SNOTEL recorded 14 inches of snow, and June Lake SNOTEL recorded 12 inches of snow.

One was clamming at Oysterville beach, the other was clamming near Warrenton Cannery Road in the community of North Cove.

Several large branches and a couple trees were downed by winds. Winds also caused power outages, with at least 5500 people losing power.  A weather station in Lake Oswego on top of Iron Mountain reported wind gusts up to 58 mph.
Salem Airport reported wind gusts up to 45 mph.  Across the Portland/Salem area, 5500 people lost power.
CoCoRaHS observer reported several trees down around town in Springfield.  The Eugene Airport ASOS recorded wind gusts of 45 to 49 mph.

CoCoRaHS observer south of Molalla reported that a few composition shingles were blown off his roof.  Another observer east of Stayton reported a power outage. A weather station in Mill City reported wind gusts up to 57 mph.
A weather station on Cape Disappointment reported wind gusts up to 65 mph.  Another weather station at Toke Point reported sustained winds up to 40 mph.
Swift Creek SNOTEL recorded 18 inches of snow, Pinto Rock SNOTEL recorded 17 inches of snow, and Lone Pine SNOTEL recorded 16 inches of snow.
Bear Grass and Red Hill SNOTELs reported 15 inches of snow, Mt Hood Meadows NWAC station recorded 18 inches of snow, and Timberline NWAC station recorded 17 inches of snow.
A Oregon DOT weather station on Megler Bridge reported wind gusts up to 61 mph.  Another weather station on Cape Disappointment reported sustained winds up to 44 mph.
A Oregon DOT weather station reported wind gusts up to 61 mph on Megler Bridge.  Another weather station across the river on Cape Disappointment reported sustained winds up to 44 mph.
Photo of funnel cloud in Lebanon shared on Twitter by KEZI Meteorologist.
Trained spotter reported a funnel cloud NE of Veneta.
Photo of funnel cloud posted to Twitter. Picture taken near Harrisburg around 310 PM.
The Grays River near Rosburg crested at 12.6 feet around 1 AM, which is 0.6 foot above flood stage. No damage was reported.

The Columbia River at Vancouver crested several times above flood stage May 17 through May 19th, with the highest crest at 16.14 feet around 8:15 AM on May 17th. This is 0.14 foot above flood stage. No damage was reported.
A trained storm spotter reported two funnel clouds 2 miles west of Brownsville, OR.
A teen on a boogie board was swept out to sea at Rockaway Beach. When his father lost sight of him, the father went into the water to find his son but never returned.  Both drowned.

A large gust of wind blew through the Harmony Sports Complex and tipped over a wooden equipment shed.  A man and young girl standing next to the shed were struck by the edge as it fell. The young girl was trapped under the shed, sustaining non-life-threatening injuries.
Oregon DOT reported debris and mud washed over highway 242 in eastern Lane County, resulting in its closure. Heavy rain over the burn area from the 2017 Separation Fire was likely the cause.
Hood River news reported that cherry, pear, and apple orchardists in the Odell area reported damage to their crop due to half-inch hail. How much damage is unknown.
Lightning struck three trees, causing two to explode. The third caught fire, then the top came crashing to the ground, landing on and damaging a deck attached to a house.
Public reported on twitter hail. The picture included a photo next to a ruler showing hail close to 1 inch in diameter.
Strong winds were reported at Rockaway Beach, just north of Garibaldi.  Strong winds of 53 knots was also reported at Clatsop Spit and Astoria.
Strong winds were reported on the Yaquina Bay Bridge along Hwy. 101 in Newport.  Strong winds of 75 knots were also reported at Florence; 70 knots at Yachats and 71 knots at Cape Foulweather.

Between 20 and 30 inches total snowfall accumulation fell, based on reports from sites such as the Mount Hood Meadows and Timberline ski resorts on Mt. Hood, the Mt. Hood Test SNOTEL site, and ODOT reports along highways 35, 20, and 26.
Six inches total snowfall accumulation was reported in Hood River as well as in Cascade Locks.
Between 18 and 22 inches total accumulated snowfall fell, based on reports from several SNOTEL sites on Mt. St. Helens, such as June Lake, Sheep Canyon, Swift Creek, and Lone Pine.
Eight inches total accumulated snowfall was recorded in Skamania.
Between 8 and 20 inches total snowfall accumulation fell, based on reports from spotters in the hills south of Hood River and in Parkdale.
Strong winds were recorded on Clatsop Spit.

Strong winds were recorded at the Sea Lion Caves, about 10 miles north of Florence.  Strong winds of 50 knots were also recorded at Florence; 51 knots at Cape Foulweather and 52 knots at Yaquina Bridge in Newport.

Tornado had estimated wind speeds of 90 to 110 mph. Damage reports along the path of the tornado include: 200+ trees down, most between 12 to 24 inches in diameter, and approximately 6 trees greater than 36 inches; 30 to 40 homes damaged, with primarily roof damage; 19 power poles were snapped off; 3 lightly constructed structures were destroyed; a parked semi-trailer was tipped over, and several dozen sculling boats were damaged near Vancouver Lake.
Temperatures on July 16th near the Sandy River in Troutdale got up to 98 degrees, the day a swimmer went underwater in the Sandy River near Glen Otto Community Park. He later died in the hospital.

A man swimming across the Willamette River from Yamhill County to Marion County near the Wheatland Ferry drowned. It had been hot the previous several days, and though temperatures were a bit cooler on the 18th with highs only in the upper 80s, it's believed that the heat over the previous several days led him to swim in the river that day.

Around 2 PM the US Coast Guard noticed a vessel had capsized while crossing the bar at the mouth of the Siuslaw River. The captain was pulled from the Ocean and later pronounced dead at the hospital. Wave heights at the time were generally around 5 to 6 feet with periods at 10 to 11 seconds, but the waves in the bar were breaking.

Standing water reported near NE 28th Ave between Glisan and Burnside. Trimet MAX lines were temporarily closed due to standing water between Lloyd Center and Hollywood.  Rain guage at the Portland Airport reported 0.82 of an inch of rain.
A dust devil developed, hitting a storage building at the Creswell Airport. The dust devil peeled back a 20-foot section of the roof.
Between 18 and 28 inches accumulated snowfall fell, based on multiple reports from ODOT stations, SNOTEL sites, and ski resorts.
Between 7 and 15 inches accumulated snowfall was reported by spotters in Cascade Locks, Hood River, and Bonneville.
Between 12 and 17 inches accumulated snowfall was reported by spotters in the hills south of Hood River and in Parkdale.
Between 6 and 10 inches accumulated snowfall was reported by spotters in Sandy, Estacada, Zig Zag, and east of Salem.
Between 4 and 10 inches total accumulated snowfall was reported by spotters in Lebanon, Lacomb, Eugene, and Springfield.

Heavy freezing rain was reported from Bonneville westward through the Columbia River Gorge. Multiple injury accidents occurred due to cars sliding on the slick roadway of I-84.  One accident was fatal, killing a 71-year old woman. She was unable to stop her van, and it slid into the back of a stopped tractor-trailer, and was eventually hit a second time by a motor home. This accident, combined with multiple others, caused I-84 to be closed for a time near Corbett.
Between 17 and 20 inches accumulated snowfall was reported by SNOTEL stations on Mt. St. Helens, such as Spencer Meadows, Sheep Canyon, and June Lake.
Twenty inches accumulated snowfall was reported in Skamania.

Between 25 and 40 inches new snowfall were reported at various stations such as ODOT stations Bennett Pass along Hwy. 35 and Government Camp along Hwy. 26, the Mount Hood Meadows and Timberline ski resorts, and the Mt. Hood Test SNOTEL site.
Twenty-eight inches new snowfall were reported at the Willamette Pass along Hwy. 58.
Between 6 and 16 inches new snowfall were reported by spotters in areas such as above 2000 feet in Oakridge, and in Vida, as well as at the McKenzie Bride ODOT station along Hwy. 126.
Thirteen inches new snowfall were reported in Parkdale.  Six inches was also reported at the Hood River Ranger Station.
Between 15 and 18 inches new snowfall were reported by ODOT stations at the Wilson River Summit as well as the Sunset Summit along Hwy. 26.
High winds were recorded on the Yaquina Bay Bridge along Hwy. 101.  High winds of 43 knots sustained and 54 knot gusts was also recorded at Florence.
High winds were recorded at Cape Foulweather.  High winds of 56 knots were also reported at Clatsop Spit.
Between 25 and 40 inches new snowfall was recorded by various SNOTEL stations on Mt. St. Helens, such as June Lake, Swift Creek, Lone Pine, and Sheep Canyon.
Eight inches new snowfall was recorded in the hills of Brush Prairie.

Between 25 and 48 inches inches new snowfall was recorded at various stations, including: Mount Hood Meadows and Timberline ski resorts, Mt. Hood Test SNOTEL site, and various ODOT reporting stations.
High winds were recorded at Cape Foulweather, a few miles south of Depoe Bay.

High winds were recorded on the Yaquina Bay Bridge along Hwy. 101 in Newport, with recorded sustained winds of 43 kt.  High winds of 38 knots sustained, 50 knot gusts was also reported at the Newport Jetty.

Forty-two inches new snowfall was recorded at the June Lake SNOTEL; 35 inches at Sheep Canyon, 34 inches at Swift Creek; 33 inches at Spencer Meadows and 31 inches at Lone Pine.  All site are on the south side of   Mt. St. Helens.

Over the course of about 18 hours, multiple avalanches occurred in the same area, over the Santiam Pass, near the intersection of Hwy. 20 and Hwy. 126. The avalanches were contributed to higher than average snow pack, and large amounts of plowed snow along the highways. The first set of avalanches occurred the morning of January 8th, the largest burying parts of US Hwy. 20 up to 15 feet deep.  Three cars were trapped by the avalanche then later freed, with no injuries.  The second round of avalanches occurred late at night on January 8th and wasn't cleared until the following morning.  Eight commercial vehicles were trapped for a time under the snow, with no injuries reported.  Both rounds closed the highways for an extended period of time for snow removal.

A couple and their young daughter took a trail down to rocks which overlook the ocean. A large wave washed over the rocks and swept the couple off the rocks and into the ocean. Both were taken to a local hospital where they were pronounced dead.
A man was swept off rocks and into the sea in Depoe Bay and died. One woman was injured walking along the beach in Lincoln City when she was hit by a wave carrying a large log.

Minor tree damage was observed several locations, including at the Portland Meadows facility, on MLK Boulevard near Union Court, and at a park along NE Bridgeton Road. Three semi-truck trailers were overturned in a parking area near Marine Drive. Minor roof damage also was noted to a building southwest of the Marine Drive and 2nd Avenue intersection.
Multiple greenhouse structures were damaged at a farm on Thatcher Road. Witness accounts also confirmed a tornado. The tornado was likely on the ground for about 30 seconds to 1 minute.

There was damage to multiple small shrubby trees just north of the railroad track along Libby Ln. There was also a sign knocked over at the NW corner of Libby Ln and Jefferson-Marion Rd, but whether or not it was caused by a tornado could not be determined. The tornado was likely on the ground for one minute or less.
A viewer sent in a photo to a local news station of a funnel cloud over the Multnomah Channel, observed around 11 AM.
Oregon DOT weather sensor measured gusts up to 78 mph on Megler Bridge. Also, in Pacific City, a weather station measured wind gusts up to 64 mph.

The Lincoln County Emergency Manager reported a home was damaged in Lincoln City.  They also lost a microwave dish on top of Otter Crest tower.  A weather station in Lincoln City measured wind gusts up to 58 mph.  A weather station on Gleneden Beach measured wind gusts up to 67 mph. Another weather station on the Yaquina Bridge measured wind gusts up to 61 mph.
A weather station on Megler Bridge measured wind gusts up to 78 mph. Another weather station on Cape Disappointment measured sustained winds up to 54 mph, with gusts up to 63 mph.
Weather station at Cape Disappointment measured wind gusts up to 66 mph.  Another weather station on Megler Bridge recorded sustained winds up to 47 mph.

Freezing rain starting the afternoon of the 11th left a layer of ice on everything, followed by 10 inches of snow overnight into the morning of the 12th.  This caused problems on ski lifts at Mt Hood Meadows the morning of the 12th, closing down ski lifts, and leaving over 150 passengers stranded. All were successfully evacuated.
Rain falling on the Eagle Creek burn scar caused a landslide that blocked exit 41 on I-84 for several days.
Weather stations on Megler Bridge and Clatsop Spit both observed sustained winds up to 43 mph.
A weather station on Yaquina Bridge recorded wind gusts up to 71 mph.  A Florence C-MAN station also recorded sustained winds up to 43 mph.

Weather stations across the Portland metro generally reported wind gusts up to 35 to 45 mph.  One weather station at Jantzen Beach reported wind gusts up to 52 mph. At least 4900 people were without power, according to PGE and Pacific Power due to downed limbs and a few downed trees on power lines.

Weather stations across the southern Willamette Valley recorded wind gusts up to 35 to 45 mph.  The strongest was at the Eugene Airport, which recorded wind gusts up to 45 mph.  Winds caused a tree to fall in Eugene, barely missing a woman who had just moved her new car out of the driveway where the tree fell.
A small funnel cloud was reported southeast of Dundee and a picture was relayed to the National Weather Service by KGW-TV.

A weather station on Cape Disappointment recorded wind gusts up to 67 mph.  Another weather station on Megler Bridge recorded sustained winds up to 43 mph.  Als, WSDOT reported a power line down on Highway 101, knocked down by strong winds.
A weather station on Megler Bridge recorded wind gusts up to 65 mph.  Winds also caused power outages impacting 209 customers in Warrenton, according to Pacific Power.

Weather stations along the central Oregon coast reported wind gusts up to 55 to 70 mph. Highest recorded was on the Yaquina Bridge, which recorded wind gusts up to 79 mph.  There were widespread power outages in Depoe Bay and Lincoln City.  ODOT reported trees down on Highway 101, Highway 229, and Route 34 at milepost 5.5.
Oregon Department of Transportation reported trees down on Highway 6 and Highway 18 through the Coast Range.  A weather station on top of Mt Hebo recorded wind gusts up to 85 mph.

A large oak tree fell on a house 2 miles NW of McMinnville. The McMinnville ASOS recorded wind gusts up to 45 mph. There were several power outages. A section of a fence was blown over 3 miles WNW of Salem.
Several power outages were reported by PGE.  Peak wind gusts of 35 to 43 mph were recorded across the Portland Metro and north Willamette Valley.

A weather station on Cape Disappointment recorded wind gusts up to 68 mph. Another weather station on Megler Bridge recorded wind gusts up to 65 mph. Toke Point RAWS also recorded sustained winds up to 44 mph.
Abernathy RAWS recorded wind gusts up to 61 mph.
The Wilson River near Tillamook crested at 12.5 feet around 10 AM, which is 0.5 foot abouve flood stage. No damage was reported.
The Grays River near Rosburg crested at 13.2 feet around 11:30 AM, which is 1.2 feet above flood stage. No damage was reported.

Over 4,000 lost power according to the Tillamook Emergency Manager. A weather station on Megler Bridge recorded wind gusts up to 75 mph.  Other weather stations recorded wind gusts up to 60 to 66 mph.
Weather stations on the Yaquina Bridge and at Gleneden Beach recorded wind gusts up to 68 mph.
The Clatskanie/Mist Emergency Manager reported several trees down in the area, including along highway 202.  Tidewater RAWS recorded wind gusts up to 68 mph.

The Echo Mountain Complex wildfire started around 2345PDT on September 7, 2020 in Lincoln County, OR, near Lat/Lon 45.015N, -123.903W.  The wildfire grew to approximately 2,550 acres before being declared officially contained on September 30, 2020. This wildfire resulted in 293 total structures lost, 22 structures damaged, and 160 residences significantly damaged. There were 1339 people evacuated at some point during the wildfire, and 1 first responder was injured.  Towns that experienced wildfire damage included Otis, Neotsu, and Rose Lodge.

The Beachie Creek wildfire started around 1100PDT on August 16, 2020 in Marion county, OR at coordinates 44.821, -122.188.   The fire grew to approximately 193,500 acres before being declared officially under control on December 2, 2020.  Destroyed were 486 residential homes, 36 non-residential commercial properties, 801 other minor structures. There were 160 structures damaged. Affected were the towns of Mill City, Gates, Lyons, and Detroit.  During this conflagration 33388 people were evacuated,  5 citizens were fatally injured; and 2 citizens and 8 responders were injured. The cause of the fire is unknown.  This fire is also known as the Santiam Fire.

The Holiday Farm wildfire started around 2020PDT on September 7, 2020 in Lane county, OR at coordinates 44.172, -122.231. A tornado occurred in Ilwaco, Washington just north of the Port of Ilwaco Airport. The tornado began near the intersection of Redwing Way and Captain Gray Drive around 1904PST, tracked northeast across a housing subdivision, crossed the Wallacut River before dissipating near the intersection of Chinook Valley Road and U.S. Highway 101 around 1908PST.  The tornado track was about one-third of a mile long and 60 yards wide.  There was minor damage to trees, fences, windows, shingles, and other unsecured attachments to structures along the path (DI 2, DOD 2).

A tornado occurred in Damascus, Oregon just south of Hwy 212 between SE Tong Road and SE 232nd Drive. Damage occurred to numerous trees, mostly small and medium size branches. There were 5 trees (all pine or poplar) that were either snapped off or uprooted. The most significant property damage was noted near Royer Road where a large poplar tree was uprooted from very wet soil. This tree landed on parked vehicles, significantly damaging three of them. No structural damage to homes, roofs, windows, or outbuildings was found.  Note: Start and end times were estimated from a combination of radar data and timestamps on videos from several members of the public who captured the event.

Strong winds and heavy snow shut down I-84 east of Troutdale.  This was a transition event, from blizzard to winter storm to freezing rain.  Mark Nelsen (KPTV Chief Met) reported 15 inches of snow total, followed by 0.75 of ice.  Sustained winds of 30-45 mph with gusts 60-80 mph were reported for 12-24 hours (or more), along with heavy snow reducing visibility to near zero during the height of the wind/snow portion of the event.  I-84 finally reopened the morning of the 14th as snow decreased and changed to a brief period of freezing rain.
A trained spotter measured 14 inches of snow in Hood River.  Certainly enough to verify a warning in the upper Hood River Valley, too.
Hood River area observed 10-16 inches of snow. A trained spotter near Hood River reported 14 inches of snow. I-84 was closed for a time.

This was a transition event for the greater Portland metro area, with wide variation in snow and ice totals across the zone.  Snowfall totals tended to be highest near the Columbia River, while the south and west metro saw much less.  General 1-4 inch snow totals in the south and west metro, but up to 10-14 inches near the Columbia, all the way down-river to Scappoose.  There was a prolonged period of freezing rain in southern portions of the metro area, resulting in massive power outages which persisted for several days in many cases.  Ice accumulations ranged from 0.25-0.50 in downtown Portland, with amounts generally increasing closer to 1 inch in the south and southeast metro.  The heaviest ice accumulations appear to have been around Oregon City, West Linn, Wilsonville, and Sherwood, where up to 1.25 inch of ice was reported.  Another slug of freezing rain came on the 14th and early 15th, this time mainly impacting downtown and eastern portions of the metro while most western areas changed over to plain rain.  This latter event was handled with a separate Ice Storm Warning.||In the Portland area over 250,000 customers across the metro area were without power due to ice, snow and winds. Key impacts included collapsed roofs and awnings, widespread tree damage, power outages, vehicle accidents, and road closures including I-84 east of Troutdale.
Snow totals ranged from around 6 inches near Prescott to 12 inches near Columbia City and St Helens.

Impacts ranged from mostly snow in the northern portion of the zone to mostly ice further south near Grand Ronde, Willamina, and the Van Duzer Corridor.  North of Highway 6, general 6 to 12 inch snow totals occurred.  South of Highway 6, precipitation was mostly in the form of freezing rain, yielding up to an inch of ice near Grand Ronde and Highway 18.  Many trees and power lines were downed by the combination of snow and ice, and many roads were closed during the event.

This was mostly an ice event for the Central Willamette Valley as a major ice storm occurred from freezing rain.  By the end of the event, there were many reports of over 1 inch of ice accumulation, with as much as 1.75 inch reported in Sheridan.  This was a crippling ice storm for the Salem metro area where generally amounts of 0.5 to 1.25 inches of ice were reported, and many were without power for days. Key impacts: widespread tree damage and power outages, including 110,000 customers without power in Salem. Multiple road closures as well including Highway 99.

events.event_narrative: Mainly for the Van Duzer (Hwy 18) corridor near Grand Ronde.  Highway 18 was closed for 24-48 hours, and ODOT pictures revealed 1.00 of ice.  A trained spotter in Blodgett (further south) also reported 0.75 of ice before it started melting the morning of the 13th.

While much of the Portland metro area was already reeling from the snow and ice event Feb 11-13, another slug of freezing rain came on the 14th and early 15th, this time mainly impacting downtown and eastern portions of the metro while most western areas changed over to plain rain.  East metro locations received generally 0.50-1.00 of ice from this second event, with amounts tapering off quickly to the south and west of Portland.  This added to the problems with power outages due to snow and ice, with estimates of 200-300k people without power in the metro area.  The ice also disrupted mass transit, shutting down the MAX system due to ice on the wires.

Wide variation of snow and ice accumulations, with impacts mainly felt near the Columbia River.  Cathlamet reported 12 inches of snow, while Astoria and Long Beach reported very little snow.  US Hwy 101 was closed at the Megler Bridge due to slippery road conditions and falling chunks of ice from the bridge structure.  Estimated ice near Astoria ranged from 0.33 to 0.66.  Similar snow and ice amounts can be assumed along both sides of the Columbia River.

Wide variety of impacts due to snow and ice, ranging from a crippling snow/ice event in the northern half, a crippling ice event in the Santiam Canyon, to minimal impacts in mostly plain rain for the extreme southern portion of the zone.  There were reports of over 2 feet of snow just east of the zone boundary, even at elevations below 2500'.  For example, a trained spotter in Detroit measured 26 inches overall, and there was a public report from Zigzag of 25 inches.

Wide variety of impacts due to snow and ice, ranging from a crippling snow event at all elevations in the northern half and elevated portions south of Santiam Canyon, a crippling snow to ice event in the Santiam Canyon.  There were several reports of 2 feet of snow within the zone.  Greatest overall total we could find was 27 inches at Mt Hood Meadows.

Snow and wind continued after the Blizzard Warning was converted to a Winter Storm Warning.  Storm total snowfall was around 24 inches at Cascade Locks by midday the 13th, and more arrived with the next impulse the 14th/15th.

Overall, ice amounts were a little less than the Oregon side of the metro area.  Totals ranged from 0.25 to 0.75, and many thousands lost power in Clark County. ||One ice-related fatality:  At 1715 PST on the 14th, one adult male, aged 57, died when he was heading southbound and lost control of his vehicle on the icy road surface, driving off the side of the Glenn Jackson Bridge near Government Island.  The vehicle and the driver's body were later found on February 17.

Strong winds and heavy snow shut down I-84 east of Troutdale.  This was a transition event, from blizzard to winter storm to freezing rain.  Mark Nelsen (KPTV Chief Met) reported 15 inches of snow total, followed by 0.75 of ice.  Sustained winds of 30-45 mph with gusts 60-80 mph were reported for 12-24 hours (or more), along with heavy snow reducing visibility to near zero during the height of the wind/snow portion of the event.  I-84 finally reopened the morning of the 14th as snow decreased and changed to a brief period of freezing rain.

Heavy snow fell through the central Columbia Gorge between the night of the 11th through the 14th. Trained spotters at Underwood and Willard measured 10-20 inches of snow. State Highway SR 14 was closed multiple days.

A winter storm brought several rounds of heavy snow and some freezing rain to the greater Vancouver area beginning the night of the 11th continuing through the 14th. This was mostly a snow event for Clark County, with snowfall amounts ranging from around 6-10 inches downtown and East Vancouver, to up to 16 inches in northern portions of the zone. Ice accumulations up to 0.5 inch was also reported in south Vancouver. Widespread transportation delays and accidents occurred, including along I-5 and I-205. Scattered power outages were also reported. Key Impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents, scattered power outages.

Widespread snow fell over the region beginning the night of the 11th and continued in waves through the 14th. Snow accumulations of 8 to 14 inches were fairly consistently reported across the zone. Widespread transportation delays occurred including along I-5. Scattered power outages were also reported.

The public reported 6.5 inches of snow in Ryderwood, Cowlitz County. A trained spotter report of 14.5 inches in the hills 4 miles NW of Castle Rock.  This is close enough to assume the Willapa Hills received similar totals.

The south Washington Cascade foothills observed heavy snowfall. A member of the public reported 11 inches in Yacolt, which is actually in far northern WAZ039 but close enough to serve as a proxy for the South Washington Cascade foothills zone.  It is likely areas closer to the Columbia Gorge received even more snow than the Yacolt report.

Wide variation of snow and ice accumulations, with impacts mainly felt near the Columbia River.  Cathlamet reported 12 inches of snow, while Astoria and Long Beach reported very little snow.  US Hwy 101 was closed at the Megler Bridge due to falling chunks of ice from the bridge structure.  Estimated ice near Astoria ranged from 0.33 to 0.66, and similar amounts can be assumed for the other side of the river.
Given the reports of 10-20 inches of snow in the Gorge, and over two feet around Mount Hood, it seems reasonable that the South Washington Cascades would see similar totals or more.

Snow and wind continued after the Blizzard Warning was converted to a Winter Storm Warning.  Storm total snowfall was around 24 inches at Cascade Locks by midday the 13th, and more arrived with the next impulse on the 14th and 15th. State Highway SR 14 was closed multiple days due to the heavy snowfall.

Nickel sized hail fell in the Warrenton area.  There were other reports of 0.25 to 0.7 inch hail in the Warrenton and Astoria at about the same time. There was one report of 0.5 inch hail covering the road up to 1 inch deep in Astoria.

The Stonewall Bank buoy (46050) reported wave heights of 24 feet at 11 seconds at 0440PST on the 5th, meeting high surf conditions.  This was the peak wave height reported.  High surf conditions ended around 0740PST on the 5th.
Weather spotter reported a gust to 54 mph which ripped a louvre door off it's hinge. The spotter believes it was a tornado, but atmospheric conditions at the time do not seem to support that idea.

A 14 year old male was reportedly swept offshore while swimming near Long Beach, Washington.  The Coast Guard Sector Columbia River and partner agencies performed search operations. After searching nearly 52 square miles, the search was suspended at|2126PST Monday.  Weather was fairly benign with general seas between 3 and 5 feet with northerly winds around 9 to 13 kts gusting  up to 17 kts. These reports are from buoy 46029.

A 6 inch diameter Aspen tree blew over the Cedar Hills neighborhood.  Other than this tree and some small branches, no other damage was noted in the neighborhood. Wind gust estimated based on damage as hourly observations in the area had gusts around 20 mph.

Record breaking temperatures for 3 days in a row. Portland International recorded high temperatures of 108, 112, and 116 F (breaking its previous all time record of 107), and low temperatures of 70, 73, and 75 F. The Oregon State Police and Oregon Medical Examiner reported 67 deaths in Multnomah County from the heat, but it is suspected this fatality count is closer to 71. There were also reports of roads buckling due to heat. Cooling shelters were opened and many businesses closed and events postponed.

The Bruler Fire was detected on July 12, 2021 and is located near the boundary between the Detroit and Sweet Home Ranger Districts near 44.591 latitude, -122.156 longitude. As of the end of July the fire burned about 200 acres.  The cause of the fire is under investigation.  The fire continued into August.

There were two consecutive days with maximum temperatures greater than 100 degrees. The hottest day was June 27 where temperatures in the area peaked around 112 degrees. Record breaking temperatures up to 111 degrees F in Eugene, OR. There were one heat related deaths reported.

An EF-0 tornado with estimated winds of 85 mph (DI:28 ,DOD:3) began near the intersection of NE 72nd Avenue and State Highway 502 at 45.7804 latitude, -122.5982 longitude. The tornado tracked in a northeast direction, ending up near NE 259th St. and NE 147th Ave at 45.8105 latitude and -122.5229 longitude.  The tornado path was about 240 yards wide with a track length of about 3.9 miles. The estimated start and end time of the tornado is 1806PST and 1821PST.  No injuries or fatalities were reported. The majority of the damage was to trees that were uprooted or snapped. Other damage included a tree that fell on an RV, and fences damaged by toppled trees.

Tidal overflow flooding occurred in the late morning through early afternoon hours on November 4th through 6th.  Fraser Road in Tillamook and the Pacific City Airport were flooded. The Garibaldi tide gage was used to determine the time the water level rose above 10.5 feet, the point at which tidal overflow usually occurs. The begin time was the first time it rose above 10.5 feet on the 4th and the end time was the last time it dropped below 10.5 feet on the 6th.

Tidal overflow flooding occurred in the late morning through early afternoon hours on 4th through 6th.  Waters covered fields around Raymond, WA. The water did not rise high enough to close highway 101. The Toke Point tide gage was used to determine the time the water level rose above 11 feet, the point at which tidal overflow usually begins. The start time was the first time it rose above 11 feet on the 4th and the end time was the last time it dropped below 11 feet on the 6th.
